proxy_language: Proto-Indo-European (late/disintegrating, as a deliberately weak stand-in); optional flavour from reconstructed Proto-Uralic/Palaeo-European hydronymy
proxy_rationale: Star Carr (c. 9000-8500 BC, Yorkshire) is known only archaeologically; no linguistic evidence survives. Indo-European is not plausibly spoken in Britain before the Neolithic-Bronze Age (c. 4000-2500 BC), and the Mesolithic language is unknown and probably unrelated to any surviving family. Because the game requires a defensible, reconstructible morphology, we use Proto-Indo-European notation as a purely conventional placeholder, with Old European-style hydronymic roots (Krahe's Alteuropaeische Hydronymie, e.g. *h2ep-, *sal-, *dru-) as the flavour layer, since river/lake/wood names are the oldest-looking stratum in British toponymy. Players should treat these names as stylised, not as claims about Mesolithic speech.
phonology: Reconstructed PIE (Fortson/Beekes conventions): stops *p *t *k *kw (*ke *g *gw), voiced aspirated *bh *dh *gh *gwh (simplify to b d g for readability if desired); fricative *s; laryngeals *h1 *h2 *h3 (often rendered with subscript numbers or dropped in game forms); resonants *m *n *l *r *y *w; vowels *e *o *a *i *u with long variants *e *o. Ablaut (e/o/zero) is productive.
phonotactics: Root shape (C)(C)eC(C); syllable nucleus is a vowel or syllabic resonant. Word-initial clusters of s + stop (*sp-, *st-, *sk-) and stop + resonant (*pl-, *tr-, *dr-, *kl-, *gr-) are allowed. Word-final is typically a short vowel or consonant (nom. *-s, *-m, *-os). No word-initial *r- is certain in many reconstructions (debated); avoid initial *r. Avoid tone; stress is mobile/accentual and not spelled.
orthography: Use plain Latin transliteration with the stem vowel and, where a reconstruction is meant, an optional leading asterisk dropped in-game. Laryngeals rendered as h (h1 -> h, h2 -> kh or h, h3 -> gh). Palatals and labiovelars simplified: k, g, kw, gw. Aspirates written bh dh gh. Hyphen allowed between compound members.
morphology: Roots take thematic (-o-/-e-) or athematic stems; nouns carry case endings (nom. -s, acc. -m, gen. -os/-es/-so for thematic nouns, loc. -i); deadjectival and abstract nouns via suffixes *-ti- (abstract), *-tor/-ter (agent), *-mo/-no- (instrument/result). Reduplication occurs in verbs, rarely in nouns. Adjectives agree with nouns; in names, bare stems or nom. forms suffice.
compounding: Root compounds (determinant + head) follow modifier-head order, with the head last and inflecting: *deru-(wood) + *wed- (water) type compounds; linking vowel -o- between members (*-o-). Genitive phrases 'X of Y' are rendered as Y-gen + X (e.g. *wodnos *ph2ter) or as compounds Y-o-X. Agent nouns: root + *-tor / *-ter ('maker/keeper'). Possessive compounds (bahuvrihi) with final stem, e.g. 'red-hand' type: *h1roudho- + *ghes-ro-.
noun_phrase_order: Adjective before noun; genitive before head noun; demonstratives before noun; no articles. In names, modifier precedes head.

worked_examples.name: seh2wel-os domos
worked_examples.gloss: seh2wel-os (sun, gen.) + domos (house) = 'house of the sun'

sources: Fortson, B. W. IV, Indo-European Language and Culture: An Introduction (2nd ed., 2010)
Beekes, R. S. P., Comparative Indo-European Linguistics: An Introduction (2nd ed., 2011)
Mallory, J. P. & Adams, D. Q., Encyclopedia of Indo-European Culture (1997)
Krahe, H., Unsere altesten Flussnamen (1964) / Alteuropaeische Hydronymie
Milisauskas, S. & Clark, J. G. D., Star Carr (1954; archaeological background only)
notes: All forms are conventional Proto-Indo-European reconstructions used as a stylistic stand-in; the actual Mesolithic language of Star Carr is unknown and probably not Indo-European. Confidence is speculative. No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word unless the language is Goidelic; this culture is not Goidelic, so forms such as wodr, kerw, deru must not be replaced by Gaelic cognates (e.g. dair, damh) in output.
